abstract: Body painting is increasingly used in anatomy education to illustrate the relationship between anatomical structures and surface landmarks. While its role in knowledge retention is documented, its contribution to soft skill development remains underexplored. This study investigated the impact of body painting on learning performance in nursing students (control group) and medical science students (study group) and explored medical science students' perceptions of soft skill development. A total of 104 nursing and 87 medical science students at Suranaree University of Technology (SUT) participated. Both groups received lectures; however, the study group additionally engaged in body painting of the muscular system. By working in pairs, students painted structures, presented their body painting work, and answered peer-generated questions. Learning performance was evaluated using mean percentage scores (MPS) from examinations, while soft skills were assessed through five-point Likert ratings, frequency analysis, and open-ended responses. Results showed a significant difference in MPS between groups for the muscular system (**p < 0.01), though smaller than the differences for other topics taught without body painting, including the skeletal system (****p < 0.0001) and cardiovascular, respiratory, and urinary systems (***p < 0.001). Among below-average students, no significant difference was observed for the muscular system, whereas significant differences persisted for other systems. The study group reported high satisfaction (4.74 ± 0.47), with interaction and collaboration rated highest (4.85 ± 0.42). Additionally, students reported perceived improvements in teamwork (92.31%) and communication skills (83.52%). These findings support body painting as an effective active learning tool that enhances knowledge retention while fostering teamwork and communication.

title: A case report on the design and implementation of a multinational blended intensive programme in clinical pharmacy practice
authors: Theo Ryan; Laura Stricker; Mya Maliyevsky; Dorine Bonte; Fabio Boylan; Giacomo Matteo Bruno; Eric Morel; Séverine Péchiné; Giovanni Ricevuti; Juliette O'Connell
venue: Currents in Pharmacy Teaching and Learning
abstract: Introduction: The development of clinical pharmacy in pharmacy education has become a key focus globally. The role of international collaboration in the evolution of clinical pharmacy has become increasingly valuable. To date, research is limited on educational programmes between countries that focus on integrating interculturality, clinical pharmacy practice, communication skills, and pharmaceutical care. Objective: This case report aims to describe a novel blended intensive programme in clinical pharmacy education and to analyse student perceptions. Methods: Three European higher education institutions (Trinity College Dublin, Université Paris-Saclay, and Università di Pavia) collaborated to create a three-year rotating blended intensive programme which included a two-week virtual component, with didactic lectures on a variety of clinical pharmacy topics, followed by a one-week in-person component, where students met at one of the universities to engage in active learning and intercultural activities. In 2025, students evaluated the programme through a survey to gain their perceptions on the experience. Results: Twenty-one students completed the survey. All students reported satisfaction with the programme in general. Based on thematic analysis of free-text responses, students reported learning more about international pharmacy practice, enjoying clinical practice activities, and suggested increased amounts of clinical practice activities in the future of the programme. Conclusion: The blended intensive programme was the first of its kind. Students reported high levels of satisfaction with the incorporation of intercultural activities and shared that this type of learning experience helped them to develop their self-perceived communication skills, teamwork, and intercultural awareness, important lessons for future similar programmes.
